name: Liberia
headline: Liberia signed its first data protection law in August 2026, but clinic records are mostly paper and a US aid deal allows patient data audits.

access.summary: No law in force that we opened gives every patient a right to see or copy their medical record. The new Data Protection Act was signed in August 2026, but its access rules are not verified, so this stays in the 15 to 35 band.
detail: The 2010 HIV and AIDS chapter of the Public Health Law says no one other than the person living with HIV may access their confidential HIV information, with exceptions. That covers one group and one kind of record, not the whole file.

A 2019 validation draft of the revised Public Health Law says each health institution must create and keep a health record for every user. It is a draft: the copy we opened is marked 'Approved XXXX, 2019' and enactment is not verified.

President Boakai signed the Data Protection Act in August 2026, according to news reports. The Act's text is behind a paywall, so whether it gives a right to a copy, with what deadline or fee, is not verified.
There is no patient portal. The Ministry of Health says most primary health centres still keep records on paper.

control.summary: Disclosing an HIV test result needs the person's prior written consent, but no general consent rule for health records was verified. A December 2025 US aid deal commits Liberia to give US officials 'any data access' for audits, with no explicit privacy safeguards.
detail: Section 18.23 of the 2010 HIV and AIDS chapter makes it unlawful to disclose a person's HIV test result to a third party without their prior written consent on a specific form. Treating staff, epidemic reporting and court orders are exceptions.

Under the US-Liberia health MOU signed on 9 December 2025, Liberia agreed to give US officials data and on-site access in up to 5 percent of facilities. Human Rights Watch says Liberia committed to provide 'any data' for abortion-rule audits without explicit privacy safeguards.
Records sit with each facility, mostly on paper. We found no opt-out, no patient-facing sharing settings and no access log anywhere in the system.

privacy.summary: Until August 2026 Liberia had no data protection law or regulator, and the new Act's rules, penalties and start date are not verified. The main health-specific protection is a 2010 HIV confidentiality rule with fines from L$1,000 and licence suspension.
detail: Section 18.26 of the HIV and AIDS chapter punishes breaches of confidentiality with a fine of at least 1,000 Liberian dollars imposed by the Ministry of Health and/or licence suspension of at least 12 months. Patients can also sue for damages.

The 2026 draft National Data Governance Policy says the data protection bill would extend the Independent Information Commission's mandate to personal data and treats health as sensitive data. Whether the signed Act kept these terms is not verified.

In June 2026 Human Rights Watch listed Liberia among countries without a binding comprehensive data protection law. The telecoms regulator fined Orange Liberia about US$21,900 in 2026 for a SIM swap privacy breach, but no health-sector case was found.
Liberia is outside the EU, so the GDPR and the European Health Data Space do not apply.

commercial.summary: We found no rule in force that limits selling health data or using it for marketing. The 2010 HIV chapter bars insurers and others with record access from disclosing records, but the new Act's commercial rules are not verified.
detail: Section 18.23(b) of the HIV and AIDS chapter makes it unlawful for health staff, recruitment agencies, insurance companies, computer operators or anyone with access to patient medical records to disclose that information.

A DLA Piper country guide says Liberia had no law defining sensitive personal data and no data protection authority before the new Act. We found no rules on health apps, data brokers or de-identified data sales.
The Data Protection Act signed in August 2026 may change this, but its text is not verified.

journey.summary: The Ministry of Health says most primary health centres keep paper records and that fragmented systems limit continuity of care. It sought a firm in June 2026 to build an EMR linked to DHIS2 and mSupply, starting with pilot sites.
detail: The Ministry's 2026 tender says paper records cause fragmented patient histories, poor data quality and delays in reporting to the national HMIS. The new EMR is to cover clinical care, pharmacy, laboratory and referrals and run offline.
The draft National Data Governance Policy says the Ministry manages health data mainly through the Health Management Information System.
Under the December 2025 US health MOU, Liberia committed to an open-source EMR in public health facilities, phased from 20 percent in 2026 to 100 percent in 2030.
Liberia has no national health insurance claims system that we could verify.

clinical.summary: A treating clinician usually sees only the paper file held at their own facility. The Ministry's planned EMR, at the tender stage in June 2026, would sync facility servers with a central server, but no shared record exists yet.
detail: The Ministry of Health says paper-based records at most primary health centres limit continuity of care. No system lets a clinician fetch a patient's history from another facility.
The planned EMR would run full copies on facility and central servers with role-based access control. It will start at selected pilot sites, and no rollout figures are published.
The 2010 HIV chapter allows health staff directly involved in treatment to see a patient's HIV information without breaching confidentiality.

research.summary: Clinical trials need written informed consent and National Research Ethics Board review, and people who withdraw decide whether their stored data may still be used. No rule on reusing records for research was verified, so two safeguards lift the base of 40 to 46.
detail: According to NIH ClinRegs, Liberia's clinical trial regulations require voluntary written consent, and participants must be told their data may be shown to the regulator and passed to sponsors without their identity.
Consent can be revoked at any time without disadvantage. On revocation, the participant decides whether their stored data may continue to be used.

The National Research Ethics Board has sole responsibility for reviewing all clinical trial protocols. The medicines regulator issued new trial and good clinical practice guidelines effective 16 April 2026.
The 2010 HIV chapter allows HIV testing of specimens for research without consent only if all identifying information is removed first.

ai.summary: Liberia has no AI law, AI regulator or clinical AI rules. The medicines regulator's 2018 guideline treats software in lab diagnostics as a device and requires approval of changes, but nothing covers AI in care.
detail: The LMHRA guideline for in-vitro diagnostics (version 002, October 2018) classifies software with the device it controls, or on its own. Any change to design or software needs LMHRA approval before use.
A June 2026 review by Levellers found no AI statute, no AI regulator and no binding AI duties in Liberia. Government activity so far is training and policy work.
Under the December 2025 US health MOU, Liberia committed to change its regulations by 31 December 2026 so US FDA approval meets LMHRA approval requirements.

news.headline: US and Liberia sign five-year, $176 million bilateral health MOU
news.why: The MOU's terms include US data access for audits and a national EMR rollout, both shaping patient records.

news.why: Advocates called for a stand-alone data protection law before health data flows abroad.

news.why: Patients may get no notice or redress when their data is accessed for US audits.
